term.name: Nonce
term.short: A nonce is a value that must not repeat within the scope defined by a cryptographic protocol, commonly under one key.
term.meta_description: Learn what a nonce is, when it must be unique or unpredictable, how it differs from a key, IV, and salt, and why reuse can break security.

body.title: Definition
body.html: A nonce is a value used once within a defined cryptographic context, often once per encryption under a particular key. It separates otherwise identical operations so they do not reuse the same internal state or keystream.

body.title: Unique does not always mean random
body.html: A nonce may be a counter, a randomly generated value with negligible collision risk, or a structured sequence. Some schemes require only uniqueness; others also require unpredictability. The algorithm or protocol defines the rule.

body.title: Nonce, IV, salt, and key
body.html: A nonce is normally public and is not a secret key. An initialization vector initializes a mode and may have stricter unpredictability requirements; in some schemes the IV is the nonce. A salt separates password derivations and may be reused only according to different rules.

faq.question: What happens if a nonce is reused?
faq.answer: The effect depends on the scheme, but it may reveal plaintext relationships, enable forgery, or completely destroy confidentiality and integrity.

faq.question: Must a nonce be random?
faq.answer: Not always. A counter can be ideal when uniqueness is guaranteed. Follow the exact requirements of the algorithm.

faq.question: How is a nonce transmitted?
faq.answer: It is commonly stored or sent alongside the ciphertext because the recipient needs it and it usually need not be secret.
